But I kept hitting the same annoyance: needing some tiny utility — convert a timestamp, resize an image, format some JSON — and every search result landing me on a bloated site drowning in ads.

articles.author: Michael Saparov
articles.description:
Tmux is a terminal multiplexer. It lets you run multiple programs in a single terminal, detach them (so they keep running in the background), and later reattach from another terminal.
Session — groups one or more windows together.
Window — groups one or more panes; a session can have multiple windows.
Pane — a split area inside a window that contains a terminal with a running program.
To start working with tmux, create a session. If you don’t specify a name, tmux will assign one automatically:
tmux

To create a session with a custom name:
tmux new -s session_name

After creating a session, tmux attaches you to automatically.
There are two ways to leave a tmux session:
Ctrl+b d

Exit the shell — the session will be destroyed if no windows remain:
Ctrl+D

To see all running sessions:
tmux ls

To attach to a session: Attach to the only (or last used) session:
tmux attach

Attach to a specific session by name:
tmux attach -t session_name

A window in tmux is similar to a tab in a terminal emulator.
To create a new window, use:
Ctrl+b c

Switch to the next or previous window:
Ctrl+b n
Ctrl+b p

Switch to a window by number:
Ctrl+b 0
Ctrl+b 1
Ctrl+b 2

Show the window list:
Ctrl+b w

A pane is a split area inside a tmux window. Each pane runs its own shell or program.
Split the current window vertically:
Ctrl+b %

Split the current window horizontally:
Ctrl+b "

Move to the next pane:
Ctrl+b o

Switch to a specific pane using arrow keys:
Ctrl+b ←
Ctrl+b →
Ctrl+b ↑
Ctrl+b ↓

Resize the current pane:
Ctrl+b Ctrl+←
Ctrl+b Ctrl+→
Ctrl+b Ctrl+↑
Ctrl+b Ctrl+↓

Close the current pane by exiting the shell:
Ctrl+D
articles.title: tmux: a modern replacement for screen

AWS Elastic Container Service (ECS) provides a built-in feature called the deployment circuit breaker, designed to make service deployments safer and more resilient.
This feature continuously monitors the health of tasks during a deployment and automatically rolls back changes if newly launched tasks fail to become healthy. When enabled, it prevents failed deployments from leaving services in a degraded or non-functional state.
Without this safeguard, deployment failures can easily go unnoticed. For example, if new tasks fail to start or never pass health checks, the service may still appear to be running while it is effectively broken. These silent failures can result in data loss, financial impact, or operational issues depending on the workload.
